130:     // The real cloud map only has a say at the very bottom of the slider. Its
131:     // contribution is crossfaded away *completely* by 15%, after which the deck is
132:     // purely procedural. Leaving any of it in shows up as rigid "chunks" of the
133:     // old map drifting through the animated clouds, because the map's own
134:     // features never move.
135:     float mapBlend = smoothstep(0.0, 0.15, uDynamics);
136:     // Raw ShaderMaterial: texture.offset is not applied for us, so the surface's
137:     // longitude shift is added here to keep the cloud map in register.
138:     float weather = texture2D(uMap, vUv + vec2(uUvOffset, 0.0)).g;
139:     float cover = mix(weather, clouds, mapBlend);
140:
141:     // --- Colour -----------------------------------------------------------
142:     // A cloud top is never a flat white. Four things shape its tone, and all of
143:     // them travel with the deck, so the tint keeps evolving as the shapes move:
144:     //
145:     //  - **Self-shadowing.** Reading the density a short way up-sun gives every
146:     //    mass a lit face and a shaded face instead of one flat tone.
147:     //  - **Optical depth.** Dense cores scatter nearly all the sunlight and read
148:     //    white; thin edges and wisps let the blue of the sky through and lean
149:     //    cool.
150:     //  - **The sun's angle.** Light raking across the deck near the terminator
151:     //    has crossed more air and warms toward sunrise orange, while the night
152:     //    side falls back to a cool ambient blue.
153:     //  - **The air mass.** A slow, large-scale field drifts subtly different hues
154:     //    between neighbouring systems.
155:     vec3 sunDirection = normalize(uSunPosition - vWorldPosition);
156:     float sunDot = dot(dir, sunDirection);
157:     float lit = smoothstep(-0.25, 0.4, sunDot);
158:     // Peaks on the terminator, where the light rakes across the cloud tops.
159:     float twilight = exp(-(sunDot * sunDot) / 0.05);
160:
161:     float alpha = cover * uOpacity * (0.12 + 0.88 * lit);
162:
163:     // The density a short step toward the sun: where it is thicker, this point
164:     // lies in the cloud's shadow. Following the sun keeps the shading correct as
165:     // the planet turns.
166:     float upSun = fbm3(p + uObjectSunDir * 0.34);
167:     float shade = mix(1.0, 0.7, smoothstep(0.36, 0.62, upSun));
168:
169:     // Regional hue: a slow field that drifts with the weather, so a big
170:     // formation is tinted unevenly instead of reading as one flat white mass.
171:     float region = fbm3(ldir * (uScale * 0.32) + vec3(uTime * 0.10, uTime * 0.04, -uTime * 0.07) + 19.0);
172:     region = smoothstep(0.32, 0.72, region);
173:
174:     // Dense, sunlit cloud is a warm white; thin or hazy cloud leans cool.
175:     vec3 warmTint = vec3(1.0, 0.978, 0.94);
176:     vec3 coolTint = vec3(0.88, 0.925, 1.0);
177:     vec3 tint = mix(warmTint, coolTint, clamp(region * 0.7 + (1.0 - cover) * 0.4, 0.0, 1.0));
178:     tint = mix(tint, vec3(1.0, 0.86, 0.7), twilight * 0.4); // sunrise / sunset warmth
179:
180:     // Held near 1 so the warm/cool tint survives instead of clipping to white.
181:     float body = mix(0.84, 1.06, cover) * shade;
182:
183:     vec3 color = uColor * tint * body * (0.24 + 0.76 * lit);
184:     // Night side: a little scattered sky light keeps the deck from going black.
185:     color += uColor * vec3(0.3, 0.38, 0.55) * (1.0 - lit) * (0.3 + 0.7 * cover);
186:
187:     gl_FragColor = vec4(color, alpha);
188:   }
189: `
190:
191: interface CloudsProps {
192:   geometry: BufferGeometry
193:   radius: number
194:   visuals: CloudVisuals
195:   sunPosition: Vector3
196:   /** 0…1 opacity multiplier from the Earth panel. */
197:   opacity: number
198:   /**
199:    * Extra rotation the deck turns through, in radians per simulated day, on top
200:    * of the planet's own spin. Positive = the clouds drift ahead of the surface.
201:    */
202:   relativeSpinPerDay: number
203:   /** 0…1 “Cloud dynamics”: scales the shape evolution only. */
204:   dynamics: number
205:   /** 0…1 cloud coverage: 0 = a few scattered wisps, 1 = a near-continuous sheet. */
206:   coverage: number
207:   reducedMotion: boolean
208:   /** Longitude shift applied to the surface, in UV turns (matches the day map). */
209:   uvOffsetU?: number
210:   /**
211:    * Extra height for the cloud shell, in planet radii, on top of the deck's own
212:    * 1.2%. Earth's surface is displaced by real relief, so the deck has to clear
213:    * the highest ground rather than the mean radius.
214:    */
215:   shellLift?: number
216: }
217:
218: export function Clouds({
219:   geometry,
220:   radius,
221:   visuals,
222:   sunPosition,
223:   opacity,
224:   relativeSpinPerDay,
225:   dynamics,
226:   coverage,
227:   reducedMotion,
228:   uvOffsetU = 0,
229:   shellLift = 0,
230: }: CloudsProps) {
231:   const meshRef = useRef<Mesh>(null)
232:
233:   const material = useMemo(
234:     () =>
235:       new ShaderMaterial({
236:         vertexShader,
237:         fragmentShader,
238:         uniforms: {
239:           uMap: { value: getTexture(visuals.textureId) },
240:           uColor: { value: new Color(visuals.color) },
241:           uSunPosition: { value: sunPosition.clone() },
242:           uObjectSunDir: { value: new Vector3(0, 1, 0) },
243:           uOpacity: { value: opacity },
244:           uTime: { value: 0 },
245:           uDynamics: { value: dynamics },
246:           uScale: { value: 2.7 },
247:           uUvOffset: { value: uvOffsetU },
248:           uCoverage: { value: coverage },
249:         },
250:         transparent: true,
251:         depthWrite: false,
252:       }),
253:     [visuals.textureId, visuals.color, sunPosition, uvOffsetU],
254:   )
255:
256:   useEffect(() => () => material.dispose(), [material])
257:
258:   // The shape-evolution clock runs in real seconds, so the clouds keep breathing
259:   // at a steady, visible pace even when the simulation is paused; it freezes for
260:   // anyone who asked for reduced motion. The relative spin, by contrast, is tied
261:   // to the simulation clock so it stays in step with the turning planet.
262:   const elapsed = useRef(0)
263:   const spun = useRef(0)
264:   const sunLocal = useRef(new Vector3())
265:   useFrame((_, delta) => {
266:     // The slider scales ONLY the shape evolution. The deck's own faster-than-
267:     // surface rotation is left alone, so at 0% the clouds still slip across the
268:     // ground while their density is frozen.
269:     if (!reducedMotion) elapsed.current += delta * dynamics
270:     spun.current += relativeSpinPerDay * clock.lastFrameDays
271:     if (meshRef.current) meshRef.current.rotation.y = spun.current
272:     material.uniforms.uTime.value = elapsed.current
273:     material.uniforms.uDynamics.value = dynamics
274:     material.uniforms.uCoverage.value = coverage
275:     material.uniforms.uOpacity.value = opacity
276:     material.uniforms.uSunPosition.value.copy(sunPosition)
277:     // The sun's direction in the deck's own space, so the shader can march a
278:     // step "up-sun" through the density field for self-shadowing.
279:     if (meshRef.current) {
280:       sunLocal.current.copy(sunPosition)
281:       meshRef.current.worldToLocal(sunLocal.current)
282:       material.uniforms.uObjectSunDir.value.copy(sunLocal.current).normalize()
283:     }
284:   })
285:
286:   return (
287:     <mesh ref={meshRef} geometry={geometry} material={material} scale={radius * (1.012 + shellLift)} />
288:   )
289: }

447:   role?: 'complementary' | 'dialog'
448:   /** 0…1 opacity of the panel's background and body. The header's controls never fade. */
449:   opacity?: number
450:   /** When supplied, an opacity slider is shown in the header while expanded. */
451:   onOpacityChange?: (value: number) => void
452:   /** Header content — the title block. Fades with the panel. */
453:   header?: ReactNode

455:   headerActions?: ReactNode

458: /**
459:  * A floating glass panel anchored to a screen edge that can be folded away.
460:  *
461:  * Expanded, it behaves like the old `Panel`/`Sheet`: a fixed, scrollable card.
462:  * Collapsed, it shrinks to a narrow vertical bar — itself a button — hugging the
463:  * edge. The width is animated with a plain CSS transition, so the browser's own
464:  * reduced-motion rules apply for free. On phones these panels are full-width
465:  * bottom sheets, so the collapsed bar is suppressed there and the panel simply
466:  * stays expanded.
467:  *
468:  * The optional opacity slider fades the panel's background and body. The header
469:  * controls — the opacity slider, the collapse chevron and any `headerActions` —
470:  * sit outside the faded layer, so they stay fully usable even at 0%. A collapsed
471:  * panel is likewise kept solid: its bar is a control.
472:  */
473: export function CollapsibleSidePanel({
474:   children,
475:   side,
476:   label,
477:   collapsedLabel,
478:   collapsed,
479:   onToggle,
480:   className = '',
481:   expandedWidthClass,
482:   collapsedWidthClass = 'w-12',
483:   bodyClassName = 'px-4 pb-4',
484:   role = 'complementary',
485:   opacity = 1,
486:   onOpacityChange,
487:   header,
488:   headerActions,
489:   ...motionProps
490: }: CollapsibleSidePanelProps) {
491:   // On the collapsed bar the chevron points away from the edge — toward the
492:   // middle of the screen — so it reads as "pull the panel back out".
493:   const expandDirection = side === 'left' ? 'right' : 'left'
494:   // A folded panel is just a handle, so it never fades; that keeps it clickable
495:   // whatever the slider was left at.
496:   const faded = collapsed ? 1 : opacity
497:   return (
498:     <motion.aside
499:       role={role}
500:       aria-label={label}
501:       {...motionProps}
502:       className={`pointer-events-auto fixed z-30 flex flex-col overflow-hidden transition-[width,top] duration-300 ease-out ${
503:         collapsed ? collapsedWidthClass : expandedWidthClass
504:       } ${className}`}
505:     >
506:       {/* The glass, on its own layer so it can fade independently of the controls. */}
507:       <div className="sse-panel absolute inset-0" style={{ opacity: faded }} aria-hidden="true" />
508:
509:       <div
510:         className={`relative flex shrink-0 items-start justify-between gap-2 px-4 pt-4 ${
511:           !collapsed && onOpacityChange ? 'pb-2' : 'pb-3'
512:         } ${collapsed ? 'sm:hidden' : ''}`}
513:       >
514:         <div className="min-w-0" style={{ opacity: faded }}>
515:           {header}
516:         </div>
517:         {/* Controls: never faded, so the panel can always be adjusted or closed. */}
518:         <div className="flex shrink-0 items-center gap-1.5">{headerActions}</div>
519:       </div>
520:
521:       {/* The opacity slider is a control, so it sits outside the faded layer too. */}
522:       {!collapsed && onOpacityChange ? (
523:         <div className="relative shrink-0 px-4 pb-3">
524:           <PanelOpacityControl value={opacity} onChange={onOpacityChange} />
525:         </div>
526:       ) : null}
527:
528:       {/* Kept mounted while collapsed (just hidden from `sm` up) so panel state
529:           and scroll position survive a fold. */}
530:       <div
531:         className={`sse-scroll relative min-h-0 flex-1 overflow-y-auto ${bodyClassName} ${
532:           collapsed ? 'sm:hidden' : ''
533:         }`}
534:         style={{ opacity: faded }}
535:       >
536:         {children}
537:       </div>
538:
539:       {collapsed ? (
540:         <button
541:           type="button"
542:           onClick={onToggle}
543:           aria-label={`Expand ${label}`}
544:           title={`Expand ${label}`}
545:           className="relative hidden min-h-0 flex-1 flex-col items-center justify-center gap-3 px-1 text-mist transition-colors hover:bg-white/6 hover:text-parchment sm:flex"
546:         >
547:           <span aria-hidden="true">
548:             <ChevronIcon size={16} direction={expandDirection} />
549:           </span>
550:           <span className="whitespace-nowrap text-[0.66rem] uppercase tracking-[0.24em] [writing-mode:vertical-rl]">
551:             {collapsedLabel}
552:           </span>
553:         </button>
554:       ) : null}
555:     </motion.aside>
556:   )
557: }

## [The GEBCO_2025 Grid | GEBCO](https://www.gebco.net/data-products-gridded-bathymetry-data/gebco2025-grid)

### Introduction

The GEBCO_2025 Grid is a global terrain model for ocean and land, providing elevation data, in meters, on a 15 arc-second interval grid of 43200 rows x 86400 columns, giving 3,732,480,000 data points. The data values are pixel-centre registered i.e. they refer to elevations, in meters, at the centre of grid cells.

The grid can be downloaded as a global file or for user-defined areas in a number of formats.

The data are available to download according to the Terms of Use.

The grid is accompanied by a Type Identifier (TID) Grid, giving information on the types of source data that the GEBCO_2025 Grid is based on.

...

### Data set reference

GEBCO Compilation Group (2025) GEBCO 2025 Grid (doi:10.5285/37c52e96-24ea-67ce-e063-7086abc05f29)

...

### GEBCO Grid, vertical and horizontal datum

The complete GEBCO_2025 data set provides global coverage, spanning 89° 59' 52.5''N, 179° 59' 52.5''W to 89° 59' 52.5''S, 179° 59' 52.5''E on a 15 arc-second geographic latitude and longitude grid. It consists of 43200 rows x 86400 columns, giving 3,732,480,000 data points. The data values are pixel-centre registered i.e. they refer to elevations, in meters, at the centre of grid cells.

The GEBCO grid can be assumed to be relative to WGS84.

...

### Data Dissemination

CF-compliant NetCDF format

The GEBCO_2025 NetCDF files are provided in NetCDF 4 format and conform to the NetCDF Climate and Forecast (CF) Metadata Convention v1.6 (http://cfconventions.org/).

Within the NetCDF files, the GEBCO_2025 gridded data are stored as a two-dimensional array of 2-byte integer values of elevation in metres, with negative values for bathymetric depths and positive values for topographic heights. The GEBCO_2025 TID grid is provided in the NetCDF format, but data are stored as a two-dimensional array of single byte integers.

- The global dataset is provided as a single 7.5 GB file
- The global TID grid is provided as a single 4 GB file

## [The GEBCO_2025 Grid - a continuous terrain model for oceans and land at 15 arc-second intervals](https://doi.org/10.5285/37c52e96-24ea-67ce-e063-7086abc05f29)
Published: 2025-08-04T00:00:00.000Z

The GEBCO_2025 Grid is a global continuous terrain model for ocean and land with a spatial resolution of 15 arc seconds. In regions largely outside of the Arctic and Southern Ocean areas, the grid uses as a base Version 2.7 of the SRTM15_plus data set (Tozer et al., 2019). This data set is a fusion of land topography with measured and estimated seafloor topography. Included on top of this base grid are gridded bathymetric data sets developed by the four Regional Centers of The Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 Project. The GEBCO_2025 Grid represents all data within the 2025 compilation. The compilation of the GEBCO_2025 Grid was carried out at the Seabed 2030 Global Center, hosted at the National Oceanography Centre, UK, with the aim of producing a seamless global terrain model. Outside of Polar regions, the Regional Centers provide their data sets as sparse grids i.e. only grid cells that contain data are populated. These data sets were included on to the base using a 'remove-restore' blending procedure. This is a two-stage process of computing the difference between the new data and the base grid and then gridding the difference and adding the difference back to the existing base grid. The aim is to achieve a smooth transition between the new and base data sets with the minimum of perturbation of the existing base data set. The data sets supplied in the form of complete grids (primarily areas north of 60N and south of 50S) were included using feather blending techniques from GlobalMapper software. The GEBCO_2025 Grid has been developed through the Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 Project. This is a collaborative project between the Nippon Foundation of Japan and the General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans (GEBCO). It aims to bring together all available bathymetric data to produce the definitive map of the world ocean floor by 2030 and make it available to all. Funded by the Nippon Foundation, the four Seabed 2030 Regional Centers include the Southern Ocean - hosted at the Alfred Wegener Institute (AWI), Germany; Pacific Ocean - hosted at the National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research (NIWA), New Zealand; Atlantic and Indian Oceans - hosted at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory (LDEO), Columbia University, USA; Arctic and North Pacific Oceans - jointly

### GEBCO_2025 Grid

A global grid at 15 arc-second intervals. Originally published in August 2025, it is the seventh GEBCO grid developed through the Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 Project.

The grid uses as a ‘base’ Version 2.7 of the SRTM15+ data set [Tozer et al 2019] largely between latitudes of 50° South and 60° North. This data set is a fusion of land topography with measured and estimated seafloor topography. This is augmented with the gridded bathymetric data sets developed by the four Seabed 2030 Regional Centers.

The data set is accompanied by a Type Identifier Grid (TID). This data set identifies the type of source data that a grid cell is based on.

Access documentation and terms of use for the grid.

- Download GEBCO_2025 Grid - ice surface elevation version, available in NetCDF, Data GeoTIFF, and ESRI ASCII raster formats
- Download GEBCO_2025 Grid - sub-ice topography version, available in NetCDF, Data GeoTIFF, and ESRI ASCII raster formats
- Download GEBCO_2025 TID Grid, available in NetCDF, Data GeoTIFF, and ESRI ASCII raster formats

ETOPO 2022 15 Arc-Second Global Relief Model

# ETOPO 2022 15 Arc-Second Global Relief Model

 Thumbnail of ETOPO

ETOPO 2022, a global relief model with 15 arc-second resolution seamlessly integrating topographic and bathymetric data. The ETOPO 2022 model uses a combination of numerous airborne lidar, satellite-derived topography, and shipborne bathymetry datasets from U.S. national and global sources. ETOPO 2022 uses bare-earth topographic data from NASAs ICESat-2 and other vetted data sources to independently validate both the input datasets and the final ETOPO 2022 model. ETOPO 2022 is available in "Ice Surface" (top of Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets) and "Bedrock" (base of the ice sheets) versions.

# ETOPO 2022 15 Arc-Second Global Relief Model

Thumbnail of ETOPO

ETOPO 2022, a global relief model with 15 arc-second resolution seamlessly integrating topographic and bathymetric data. The ETOPO 2022 model uses a combination of numerous airborne lidar, satellite-derived topography, and shipborne bathymetry datasets from U.S. national and global sources. ETOPO 2022 uses bare-earth topographic data from NASAs ICESat-2 and other vetted data sources to independently validate both the input datasets and the final ETOPO 2022 model. ETOPO 2022 is available in "Ice Surface" (top of Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets) and "Bedrock" (base of the ice sheets) versions.

These models were released using predicted bathymetry generated using three versions of the marine gravity model (V7, V11, and V24) which had significant improvements owing to increases in altimetry data volume and accuracy (Table 1 and Figure 2). ## [The GEBCO_2024 Grid](https://www.gebco.net/data-products-gridded-bathymetry-data/gebco2024-grid)

The GEBCO_2024 Grid is a global terrain model for ocean and land, providing elevation data, in meters, on a 15 arc-second interval grid of 43200 rows x 86400 columns, giving 3,732,480,000 data points. The data values are pixel-centre registered i.e. they refer to elevations, in meters, at the centre of grid cells.

...

The grid was published in July 2024 and is the sixth GEBCO grid developed through The Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 Project. This is a collaborative project between the Nippon Foundation of Japan and GEBCO. The Seabed 2030 Project aims to bring together all available bathymetric data to produce the definitive map of the world ocean floor and make it available to all.

...

### Grid development

The GEBCO_2024 Grid is a continuous, global terrain model for ocean and land with a spatial resolution of 15 arc seconds. It uses as a ‘base’ version 2.6 of the SRTM15+ data set between latitudes of 50° South and 60° North. This data set is a fusion of land topography with measured and estimated seafloor topography. This version of SRTM15+ is similar to version 2.1 [Tozer et al., 2019] but includes additional data sets. It uses predicted depths based on the V32 gravity model [Sandwell et al., 2019].

...

### GEBCO Type Identifier (TID) Grid

The GEBCO Grid is accompanied by a Type Identifier (TID) grid. This data set identifies the type of source data that the corresponding grid cells in the GEBCO Grid are based on. Further information about the format and coding of the TID grid is given below.

| TID | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Land |
| Direct measurements | |
| 10 | Singlebeam - depth value collected by a single beam echo-sounder |
| 11 | Multibeam - depth value collected by a multibeam echo-sounder |
| 12 | Seismic - depth value collected by seismic methods |
| 13 | Isolated sounding - depth value that is not part of a regular survey or trackline |
| 14 | ENC sounding - depth value extracted from an Electronic Navigation Chart (ENC) |
| 15 | Lidar - depth derived from a bathymetric lidar sensor |
| 16 | Depth measured by optical light sensor |
| 17 | Combination of direct measurement methods |
| Indirect measurements | |
| 40 | Predicted based on satellite-derived gravity data - depth value is an interpolated value guided by satellite-derived gravity data |
| 41 | Interpolated based on a computer algorithm - depth value is an interpolated value based on a computer algorithm (e.g. Generic Mapping Tools) |
| 42 | Digital bathymetric contours from charts - depth value taken from a bathymetric contour data set |
| 43 | Digital bathymetric contours from ENCs - depth value taken from bathymetric contours from an Electronic Navigation Chart (ENC) |
| 44 | Bathymetric sounding - depth value at this location is constrained by bathymetric sounding(s) within a gridded data set where interpolation between sounding points is guided by satellite-derived gravity data |
| 45 | Predicted based on helicopter/flight-derived gravity data |
| 46 | Depth estimated by calculating the draft of a grounded iceberg using satellite-derived freeboard measurement. |
| Unknown | |
| 70 | Pre-generated grid - depth value is taken from a pre-generated grid that is based on mixed source data types, e.g. single beam, multibeam, interpolation etc. |
| 71 | Unknown source - depth value from an unknown source |
| 72 | Steering points - depth value used to constrain the grid in areas of poor data coverage |

## [Seabed 2030 announces latest progress on World Hydrography Day | Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission](https://www.ioc.unesco.org/en/articles/seabed-2030-announces-latest-progress-world-hydrography-day)
Published: 2024-06-21T13:27:53.000Z

21 June 2024 Last update: 16 October 2025

On the occasion of World Hydrography Day, The Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 Project has announced the latest percentage of ocean floor mapped, marking an increase of 4.34 million square kilometres of new data – equating to an area the size of the European Union. The global effort to compile a definitive map of the world’s entire ocean floor is being spearheaded by Seabed 2030 – a collaborative project between The Nippon Foundation and the General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans (GEBCO), with the latter being a joint programme of the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) and the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission (IOC) of UNESCO. Seabed 2030 is also a flagship programme of the Ocean Decade – a framework to create a sustainable and well managed ocean. The latest figure of 26.1% mapped is a testament to the continuous efforts and advancements in seafloor mapping technologies and activities. While the increase showcases progress in the portion of the seabed mapped, it’s important to highlight the remarkable discoveries made possible through this global effort to uncover Earth’s final frontier – discoveries that are essential for realising sustainable ocean management. In the past year alone, ocean research has led to the characterisation of the largest known deep-sea coral reef habitat off the southeast U.S. coast. The multi-year campaign to map and explore this region was led by Seabed 2030 partner National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Ocean Exploration, in collaboration with a host of other government, academic, and private sector collaborators. The analysis of newly-mapped seafloor revealed an extensive coral habitat spanning over 6.4 million acres on the Blake Plateau. "This strategic multi-agency effort to systematically map and characterise the stunning coral ecosystem right on the doorstep of the U.S. East Coast is a perfect example of what we can accomplish when we pool resources and focus on exploring the 74% of global marine waters that are still unmapped," said Derek Sowers, lead author of the study and Mapping Operations Manager at Ocean Exploration Trust. Advanced sonar and imaging techniques documented 83,908 coral mounds, showcasing the immense biodiversity previously unknown in this region. This discovery, supported by imagery from 23 submersible dives, highlights the critical role of seafloor mapping in revealing previously unknown aspects of the ocean. In another remarkable finding, the crew aboard the Schmidt Ocean Institute’s research vessel Falkor (too) made a groundbreaking discovery of four underwater mountains, with the tallest of these standing over 1.5 miles high, using multibeam mapping techniques. These seafloor features, revealed during a transit from Golfito, Costa Rica, to Valparaiso, Chile, had not been previously recorded in any bathymetric database. Additionally, scientists aboard the Schmidt Ocean Institute research vessel Falkor (too) have identified over 100 potential new marine species during a single deep-sea expedition, highlighting the vast, untapped biodiversity of the ocean. Executive Director of Schmidt Ocean Institute Jyotika Virmani commented: "What lies beneath the waves is the largest mystery on our planet and the ocean continues to reveal magnificent new surprises. Schmidt Ocean Institute is proud to be a partner of The Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 Project and a part of the phenomenal international effort currently underway to map our entire planet for the first time in human history." These findings underscore the vital importance of seabed mapping in enhancing our understanding of marine ecosystems and informing frameworks for sustainable management.

## [Frontiers | Status of global seafloor mapping effort and priority areas for future mapping](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1543885/full)
Published: 2025-05-30T20:15:13.000Z

Meanwhile, the availability of optical satellite imagery, usually from multispectral sensors, also advanced seafloor mapping techniques through satellite-derived bathymetry (SDM), offering an alternative to acoustic bathymetric methods in coastal areas, shallow seas and lakes (Jupp, 1988; Laporte et al., 2023). Additionally, scientists began using satellite altimetry to map the seafloor indirectly through measurement of small variations in sea surface height, which correlate with gravity anomalies created by underwater features (Sandwell et al., 2006; Tozer et al., 2019). Furthermore, 21st-century advances have enabled the application of autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) to acquire ultra high-resolution seafloor depth information over specific geographic areas. More recently, crowdsourced bathymetry is now an important part of the global ocean mapping campaign and has been encouraged by the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO), facilitating mariners, amateur and professional, to contribute bathymetric data (https://seabed2030.org). Accuracy, detection range, resolution and coverage of all the seafloor mapping methods strongly depends on environmental conditions such as depth, water clarity, and other physical properties of the water column, and technical parameters such as frequency, beam width, and platform stability. The performance of data acquisition devices for seafloor mapping and model accuracy was reviewed in detail by Li et al. (2023).

...

Since the inception of the Seabed 2030 project, significant progress has been made in increasing the proportion of measured versus estimated seafloor area, rising from 6.2% in 2014 (GEBCO_2014 grid, the product preceding the start of Seabed 2030) to 15% in 2019 (GEBCO_2019 grid, the first Seabed 2030 grid) to 26.1% in 2024 (current GEBCO_2024 grid) (Weatherall et al., 2015; Mayer et al., 2018; Wölfl et al., 2019; Seabed 2030 Project, T. N. F, 2024). Yet over 70% of the world’s ocean is not mapped by high-resolution bathymetric data. In the GEBCO bathymetric grids, the areas not comprising directly measured data are infilled by indirect measurements such as satellite altimetry data (i.e., the SRTM15+ data set), interpolation or bathymetric contours from charts (Smith and Sandwell, 1997; Weatherall et al., 2015; Tozer et al., 2019). Although the predicted DBM from indirect methods gives the general trend of the seafloor morphology such as mid-ocean ridges and fracture zones, its accuracy and reliability is limited for finer-scale features such as submarine canyons and seamounts (Beaman et al., 2010; Klein et al., 2023). Several studies have subsequently used crowd-sourced bathymetry or algorithms with ship-borne ground-truth data to improve the accuracies of these global elevation grids in production of local scale maps (Novaczek et al., 2019; Jakobsson et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2020; Dorschel et al., 2022).

This study employed a systematic geospatial workflow to analyse the GEBCO global bathymetric and Type Identifier (TID) grid raster data from 2019 to 2024 within specific depth zones across different ocean basins, seas, EEZs, ABNJ, and the increment of areal coverage of seafloor that is considered mapped. The TID grids give information on the types of source data that the GEBCO compilations are based on (www.gebco.net/data_and_products/historical_data_sets). The term ‘mapped area’ has different

...

There has been a significant increase in the seafloor area mapped by direct measurement over the past six years, and MBES remained as the most used mapping method. In 2019, only 12.4% of the world’s seafloor was mapped, of which 12.2% was mapped by MBES (Figure 2, Supplementary Table S3). Since then, there has been a consistent increase each year in both direct measurement and area mapped with MBES. The growth is steady, and the areal coverage of 2024 is over twice that of 2019. Specifically, directly mapped area increased to 28.5% in 2024, of which 24.2% was mapped through MBES. The incremental increase for direct measurement ranges between 3-4% (average 3.2%) of global seafloor area each year, while the annual increment for MBES is smaller at about 2-3% (average 2.5%). This higher increase in the proportion of direct measurement area compared to the increase in MBES coverage is perhaps due to the wider application of Lidar and satellite-derived bathymetry in shallow zones, as well as the release of commercial seismic-derived bathymetric datasets in recent years (Lebrec et al., 2021; Harishidayat et al., 2024) (Figure 2b).

...

### Why direct mapping matters

Differences between unmapped (where existing bathymetry has only been predicted by interpolation and indirect depth measurements) and mapped (where bathymetry is derived from direct mapping methods) areas were assessed using a depth difference map generated by subtracting the unmapped area (covered by the SRTM15+ model) of the GEBCO_2022 bathymetry grid from the mapped (measured) area in the GEBCO_2024 bathymetry grid. The GEBCO_2022 TID grid was selected to evaluate the depth discrepancy to avoid TID mis-categorisation present in the previous TID grids.

Overall, the vast majority (85.7%) of the predicted depths deviate from the measured depths by no more than ±100 m, suggesting the SRTM15+ model is consistent with its estimated level of accuracy in these areas (Figure 9a). The depth differences are within 100 to 500 m in 14% of the compared area, and considering the full depth of the ocean, this difference could be deemed minor, especially in the abyssal and hadal zones. Depth differences in the remaining 0.3% mostly range between 500 to 2000 m. Within the 0–500 m offset range, the measured depth value was deeper than the predicted value in 62.1% of the cases, and shallower than the predicted value in 37.6% of the cases (Figure 9a).

Figure 9

Differences in depth value from the mapped and unmapped grids, calculated by subtracting GEBCO_2022 grid from the GEBCO_2024 grid for the specific area that is considered unmapped in in the former and mapped in the latter compilation. (a) Distribution histogram showing the depth differences and corresponding area. (b) Distribution histogram showing the depth maximum, minimum and average differences within specific depth intervals.

However, discrepancies between the depth value of the unmapped and directly mapped areas are depth-dependent (Figure 9b). The absolute average differences between mapped and predicted grids increase from less than 3 m in the shallow and upper bathyal zone (200–1000 m), to an extreme of 4161 m in depths greater than 10,000 m (Figure 9b). Although the predicted and mapped depth values are comparable for shallower depths, average absolute depth differences start to increase at hadal depths, indicating increased discrepancy between indirectly and directly mapped depth values in deeper waters. Across all depths, outliers can be found in either direction though trending towards deeper measured values with depth.

## [Release of the GEBCO_2025 Grid | GEBCO](https://www.gebco.net/news/release-gebco2025-grid)
Published: 2025-08-06T00:00:00.000Z

The GEBCO grid is global data set of elevation values, in metres, on a 15 arc-second interval grid.

The grid is developed through the Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 Project. This is a collaborative project between the Nippon Foundation of Japan and GEBCO. Seabed 2030's mission is to inspire ocean mapping and deliver a complete seabed map for the benefit of people and the planet.

For this release of the GEBCO grid, 27.3% of the world’s ocean floor has now been mapped to modern standards compared with 26.1% for the previous release in 2024.

    Collection Overview:


    The global bathymetry and topography grid at 15 Arc Sec is the latest iteration of the SRTM+ digital elevation model (DEM) where the "plus" indicates the addition of ocean bathymetry from shipboard soundings and satellite-derived predicted depths.  This DEM is a global elevation grid with a spatial sampling interval of 15 arc seconds (approximately 500 x 500 m pixel size at the equator).   New data consists of >33.6 million multibeam and singlebeam measurements collated by several institutions, namely, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, Geoscience Australia, Center for Coastal and Ocean Mapping, and Scripps Institution of Oceanography. New altimetry data consists of 48, 14, and 12 months of retracked range measurements from Cryosat-2, SARAL/AltiKa, and Jason-2, respectively.  Onshore, topography data are sourced from previously published digital elevation models, predominately SRTM-CGIAR V4.1 between 60N and 60S. ArcticDEM is used above 60N, while Reference Elevation Model of Antarctica is used below 62S.   For more information on this dataset, see its associated publication:   Tozer, B, Sandwell, D. T., Smith, W. H. F., Olson, C., Beale, J. R., & Wessel, P. (2019). Global bathymetry and topography at 15 arc sec: SRTM15+. Earth and Space Science, 6, 1847. https://doi.org/10.1029/2019EA000658  or visit the project website here for more details.OpenTopography enabled access to version 2.5.5 of this dataset on November 6th 2023. Previous to this date, OpenTopography was supplying V2.1

# Feasibility & Implementation Plan — Adjustable Seawater Opacity + Seafloor Topography

## 1. What the codebase actually is (verified)

**Stack (verified in `package.json`, `vite.config.ts`, `tsconfig.json`)**
React 19.2 + TypeScript (strict) + Vite 8, `three@0.186`, `@react-three/fiber@9`, `@react-three/drei`, `@react-three/postprocessing`, `zustand@5`, `framer-motion`, Tailwind 4. Tests run with Node's built-in runner (`node --test tests/`). Targets WebGL 2, with a 2D orrery fallback.

**How Earth is rendered (verified in `src/components/3d/Planet.tsx`, `src/data/visuals.ts`)**
- Earth is **one** `MeshStandardMaterial` sphere (`surfaceMaterial`) — `map` = 8K day map, `roughnessMap` = derived ocean/land roughness, plus a `bumpMap`.
- **There is no separate ocean mesh or water volume.** "Ocean" is simply the blue pixels of the day map on that single mesh.
- Relief is real: the vertex shader is patched via `material.onBeforeCompile` (`src/components/3d/terrain.ts`, `TERRAIN_VERTEX_DISPLACE`) to displace vertices from an 8‑bit grayscale DEM (`public/textures/earth_heightmap.jpg`, 3840×1920).
- **Verified by direct pixel inspection of `earth_heightmap.jpg`:** every sampled ocean point (mid-Pacific, Mariana Trench, Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Arctic) is exactly `RGB(12,12,12)`. The DEM is land-only; **the oceans are a flat sphere at mean radius** (`terrain.ts` sets the bias so sea level = radius 1). So the existing DEM cannot be reused for seafloor topography.
- The water/land mask is already computed in JS (`analyseEarth` / `waterMaskFromImage` → `earthRoughness`, green channel ≈26/255 water, ≈235/255 land) and uploaded as a **data** map (no sRGB decode). This is a ready-made water mask.
- All Earth maps share one longitude offset `textureOffsetU = 0.55` and an equirectangular 2:1 projection (verified: Everest at lon 87° lands on the bright pixel in the DEM).
- Shells (`Atmosphere`, `Clouds`, `NightLights`) are additive, `depthWrite:false`, and lifted by `terrain.peakRadius`. `NightLights` shares the terrain uniforms.

**Texture pipeline (verified in `src/utils/textures.ts`, `textureSources.ts`, `textureResolution.ts`)**
- Files live in `public/textures`, loaded before the scene mounts; progress on the loading screen. Quality tiers scale uploads ×1 / ×0.5 / ×0.25; per-map ceilings via `TEXTURE_MAX_WIDTH`; clamped to `maxTextureSize()`.
- Data maps (`earthClouds`, `earthRoughness`, `earthHeightmap`) are uploaded `NoColorSpace`.
- If a file is missing/fails to decode, a **procedural painter** is used so nothing renders blank; `getTexture()` otherwise returns a 4×4 `#404040` fallback.

**Info panel / store / config / i18n (verified)**
- `src/components/ui/PlanetPanel.tsx` renders Earth-only sections using `SliderRow` (`src/components/ui/primitives.tsx`).
- `src/store/simulationStore.ts` holds `earthAtmosphereOpacity`, `earthCloudOpacity`, `earthCloudDynamics`, `earthCloudCoverage`, `earthTerrainRelief`; each has a setter, is in `SettingsPatch`, `initialState`, and `applySettings`.
- `src/config/appConfig.ts` + `public/config.jsonc` define validated, documented settings applied before first render.
- `src/i18n/en.ts` is the source of truth; `zh.ts` is typed `Record<TranslationKey, string>` — **adding an English key without a Chinese one is a compile error.**

**Feasibility verdict:** Feasible and well-supported by the existing architecture. The terrain-displacement mechanism, the water mask, the data-texture path, the slider/config/i18n pattern, and the quality-tier system all already exist. The main new work is (a) sourcing/encoding a bathymetry texture and (b) one shader extension on the existing surface material. No new transparent pass or mesh is required for the MVP.

## 3. Rendering approach evaluation

The three options in the request, judged against this architecture:

1. **Basic transparency (fade the ocean material's opacity).** ❌ Risky here. The ocean is not a separate material; making it transparent means either a transparent pass on the whole Earth mesh (changes the 100% look, breaks front/back-face self-occlusion, interacts with clouds/atmosphere depth sorting) or splitting the mesh into land + water layers (a large rewrite). It also cannot guarantee an unchanged 100% appearance.
2. **Depth-aware visibility (blend by water depth).** ✅ Cheap and physically motivated; a good enhancement layered on the MVP.
3. **Physically informed (Beer–Lambert absorption + scattering + view distance).** ✅ Feasible in-shader but harder to validate and to keep "predictable". → optional later enhancement.

**Recommended MVP: single-mesh, shader-blended seafloor ("drain/morph"), implementing the requested formula exactly.**
Keep the existing surface mesh. Add a bathymetry height field and, for **ocean pixels only**, gate a downward displacement and a colour/roughness blend on the slider. At 100% the seafloor contribution is *exactly zero*, so the appearance is pixel-identical to today; at 0% the ocean floor is displaced to true (exaggerated) depth and coloured by a depth ramp. This:
- needs **no** new mesh, **no** transparent pass, and **no** draw call;
- sidesteps transparency sorting, depth-test and self-occlusion entirely;
- implements the requested `O = S/100, V = 1−O` literally.

Its one honest limitation (to document): it is a *crossfade/morph*, not a volumetric water layer, so intermediate values don't show true water-above-floor parallax. At globe scale the water column is ~0.17% of the radius, so parallax is negligible. A true translucent water shell is proposed as an optional enhancement (P2).

**Shading math (MVP)**
- Decode depth from the bathymetry texel; `O = S/100`, `V = 1−O`.
- Vertex: `seaOffset = −depthFraction · uBathyScale · V`, where `uBathyScale = (maxDepthM / EARTH_RADIUS_M) · exaggeration`. Added to the existing land displacement. At `V=0` → 0.
- Fragment (after `map_fragment`): `reveal = waterMask · V`; `diffuseColor.rgb = mix(dayColor, seafloorRamp(depth), reveal)`; and after `roughnessmap_fragment`: `roughnessFactor = mix(roughnessFactor, seafloorRoughness, reveal)` so the water's sun-glint fades as it drains.
- `waterMask` is reused from the existing `earthRoughness` green channel (`water = 1 − green`), applied with the shared UV offset — zero new cost. (A dedicated mask texture is a clean alternative.)
- Optional depth-aware tweak (P1): `reveal = waterMask · V · exp(−depth · k · O)` — still exactly 1 at `V=1`, still 0 at `V=0`, but deep floor stays hidden at mid values.

**Vertical exaggeration:** reuse the existing `Terrain relief` slider so one control governs both land and sea (`exaggeration = terrain.maxExaggeration · earthTerrainRelief`). At `relief=0` the floor is flat but still depth-coloured. (A separate seafloor exaggeration is the alternative.)

## 6. Risks, dependencies, data storage

**Risks / mitigations**
- *Alignment/projection mismatch* (seafloor offset from coastlines): ETOPO/GEBCO and the DEM are both standard equirectangular, so it should align automatically; **verify** with known features (Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Mariana Trench, shelf edges) and the project's existing zero-shift/PSNR method. Watch for half-pixel registration differences (negligible at 4096).
- *100% not unchanged*: guaranteed by `V=0` → zero displacement and `reveal=0`; validate by screenshot pixel-diff.
- *JPEG terracing on a heightfield*: use **PNG** (lossless), unlike the land DEM's JPEG.
- *8‑bit quantization*: 0–11,034 m → ~43 m/level; sub-pixel after exaggeration. Use a sqrt encoding to protect shallow shelves; 16‑bit is a P2 option.
- *Missing/failed data*: procedural fallback = flat sea level + `hasTexture` gate → slider goes inert, no crash, no invented terrain.
- *Transparency/sorting*: avoided by the single-mesh design (the P2 shell reintroduces it deliberately).
- *Performance*: +1 texture and a few sampler fetches, no new draw calls, no new pass; the slider writes a uniform only.
- *Over-claiming accuracy*: UI hint and comments state ~73% predicted and that the slider is nominal, not physical transmission.

**Dependencies:** a build-time GeoTIFF decode (recommend `geotiff` as a **devDependency**, used only by `tools/fetch-bathymetry.mjs`; a GDAL/Python alternative avoids any new dependency). No runtime dependency added.

**Data storage:** raw ETOPO 60″ GeoTIFF ≈ **456 MB, download-only, not committed**; committed `earth_bathymetry.png` at 4096×2048 ≈ **4–10 MB** (or ~1–2 MB at 2048×1024); GPU ≈ 8 MB + mipmaps at 4K. ETOPO is CC0; GEBCO is public domain with attribution requested.

Let me lay out pros/cons.

Option A: Node script (`tools/fetch-bathymetry.mjs`) using `geotiff` (npm) + Node's built-in `zlib` to write PNG.

- Matches the existing `tools/fetch-textures.mjs` pattern exactly (same repo, same language, same `npm` workflow, one command).
- Reproducible by anyone with Node (already required for the project).
- `geotiff` is pure JS/WASM (no native build), works cross-platform, reads ETOPO/GEBCO GeoTIFFs and supports windowed/decimated reads (important for big files — you can read at a reduced resolution without loading everything).
- Self-documenting provenance; can regenerate and update CREDITS.md automatically.
- No external toolchain for contributors.
Cons:
- Adds a devDependency (`geotiff`, ~a few hundred KB, dev-only, not in the app bundle).
- Decoding a 7.5 GB GEBCO netCDF isn't supported by `geotiff` (it's GeoTIFF-only); we'd need GeoTIFF tiles or the `netcdfjs` package for netCDF. ETOPO 60″ GeoTIFF works directly.
- Writing PNG by hand (or via a small lib) is a bit of code; `geotiff` doesn't write PNG. Could use `pngjs` or a ~60-line built-in zlib encoder.

Option B: Offline GDAL/Python (gdal_translate / gdalwarp / Python + rasterio/xarray).
Pros:
- The gold standard for geospatial: `gdalwarp`/`gdal_translate -outsize` can reproject, resample, and encode in one line; handles netCDF and GeoTIFF and multi-GB files efficiently (streaming/tiling).
- No new npm dependency; the app repo stays dependency-clean.
- Can produce exactly the equirectangular PNG with a color/format spec easily.
- Handles GEBCO's 7.5 GB netCDF gracefully (windowed reads).
Cons:
- Requires the contributor to install GDAL/Python (not part of the Node workflow); not reproducible with a single `npm` command.
- Platform setup friction (Windows GDAL installs can be fiddly).
- Less discoverable / less "in-repo" than a Node script; the generation steps live in docs rather than executable code.
- Doesn't integrate with `CREDITS.md` regeneration as naturally (though a small Node wrapper could).

Recommendation: **Option A (Node script with `geotiff` devDependency)**, because:
- It matches the repo's established convention (`tools/fetch-textures.mjs`), keeps provenance executable and reproducible with `npm`, and `geotiff` reads ETOPO's GeoTIFF with windowed/decimated access so even large tiles are memory-safe.
- The only new thing is a dev-only dependency + a tiny PNG writer.
- If we later want GEBCO netCDF or the 7.5 GB file, `gdal`/`netcdfjs` can be added then; but with ETOPO 60″ (single 456 MB GeoTIFF) the Node path is simple.

## Decision 1 — GEBCO_2025 size and your hardware

**First, an important separation of concerns.** There are two completely different "sizes" in play:

- **Build-time / preprocessing** (downloading and decoding the source grid into a PNG). This is a *one-off* on a development machine.
- **Runtime** (what the browser app loads). The app **never** loads GEBCO or ETOPO — only the derived grayscale PNG (a few MB). So the source dataset's size has **zero** effect on your RX 6650 XT / 16 GB runtime.

**GEBCO_2025 15″ size (verified):**
- Global NetCDF: **7.5 GB** (43,200 × 86,400 int16 = 3.73 billion cells), plus an optional **4 GB** TID grid.
- Or **8 tiles** of 90°×90° (GeoTIFF/ASCII), each ≈933 MB uncompressed.

**Your machine, if you did choose GEBCO 15″:**
- *Runtime:* trivially fine — the app would only hold an 8192×4096 bathymetry texture (~45–180 MB VRAM depending on format; see decision 2). 8 GB VRAM is ample.
- *Preprocessing:* 16 GB RAM **can** handle 7.5 GB, but only if processed **tile-by-tile / windowed** (≤~1 GB live at a time). A naive "read the whole global grid" would be risky at 16 GB. You'd also need ~8 GB free disk.

**But you don't need 15″ for this feature.** The math (verified by calculation):
- An 8192×4096 texture = 0.0439°/px = **158 arc-sec per output pixel**.
- 60″ source = 1.67×10⁻² ° → you're **downsampling by ~2.6×**. So 60″ already carries ~2.6× more detail than 8192 can show.
- 15″ source would be **~10.5× oversampled** — pure waste. And the *real* resolution of the seafloor data is ~6 km (satellite-predicted) anyway, which 60″ (~1.85 km) already captures.

**Recommendation:** **ETOPO 2022 60″** — a single **456 MB** GeoTIFF, **CC0**, and visually identical to GEBCO 15″ at any texture size this app will ship. GEBCO and ETOPO share the same SRTM15+ ocean base, so the floor shapes are essentially the same; GEBCO's advantage (newer regional multibeam) is invisible below ~5 km/px. Keep GEBCO_2025 as the documented authoritative cross-check, not the build source.

---

## Decision 2 — 8192×4096 / 4096×2048 (default) / 2048×1024

**Yes — this is exactly the existing pattern and it works cleanly.**

Ship the bathymetry source at 8192×4096 with **no `TEXTURE_MAX_WIDTH` ceiling** (unlike the land DEM's 2048 cap). `textureUploadWidth()` in `src/utils/textureResolution.ts` then produces precisely:

| Tier | Uploaded | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| High | 8192×4096 | decoded `<img>` uploaded directly (no canvas copy) |
| **Medium (store default)** | **4096×2048** | matches `quality: 'medium'` in the store |
| Low | 2048×1024 | |
| any | clamped to `maxTextureSize()` | safe on weak drivers |

VRAM (verified arithmetic):

| Tier | RGBA (three.js default) + mips | Single-channel R8 + mips |
|---|---|---|
| 8192×4096 | ~134 MB → ~179 MB | ~34 MB → ~45 MB |
| 4096×2048 | ~34 MB → ~45 MB | ~8 MB → ~11 MB |
| 2048×1024 | ~8 MB → ~11 MB | ~2 MB → ~3 MB |

Your GPU handles the High RGBA case easily (the app already spends ~179 MB each on the 8K day and night maps). As a P1 optimization I'd set `texture.format = RedFormat` to cut it to ~45 MB (WebGL2 supports R8 uploads from DOM sources; fall back to RGBA if a driver misbehaves).

Two asset caveats to be aware of:
- The committed 8192×4096 **PNG** will be roughly **8–30 MB** (lossless; avoids JPEG terracing on a height field). WebP-lossless is an option to shrink it. If that's too big for the repo, we could drop the *source* to 4096×2048 (High = 4096) — but I'd keep 8192 since it does resolve the ~6 km predicted detail better.
- Preprocessing a 8192×4096 output from a 60″ grid is trivial (source ~466 MB in memory).

## Decision 5 — Preprocessing dependency: Node + `geotiff` vs. offline GDAL/Python

| | **A. Node script + `geotiff` devDependency** | **B. Offline GDAL/Python** |
|---|---|---|
| **Repo fit** | ✅ Mirrors the existing `tools/fetch-textures.mjs` exactly — same language, same `npm` workflow, one command | ❌ Steps live in docs, outside the repo's tooling |
| **Reproducibility** | ✅ Anyone with Node (already required) can regenerate | ❌ Requires installing GDAL/rasterio first |
| **Memory safety on big grids** | ✅ `geotiff` supports windowed/decimated reads (read only the resolution you need) | ✅ GDAL streams/tiles natively |
| **Formats** | ✅ ETOPO 60″ **GeoTIFF** works directly. ❌ Can't read GEBCO **NetCDF** (would need `netcdfjs`) | ✅ Both GeoTIFF and NetCDF |
| **Resample/reproject** | ⚠️ You write the resample loop yourself (simple: it's already equirectangular, just area-average) | ✅ `gdal_translate -outsize` / `gdalwarp` in one line |
| **PNG writing** | ⚠️ Needs a small writer (`zlib` built-in, ~60 lines) or `pngjs` | ✅ `-of PNG` built in |
| **Dependencies added** | 1 dev-only package (`geotiff`, not in the app bundle) | none in-repo |
| **Windows friction** | ✅ none (pure JS/WASM) | ⚠️ GDAL installs can be fiddly |
| **CREDITS.md regeneration** | ✅ automatic, in-script | ❌ separate step |

**Recommendation: Option A**, because it matches this repo's established convention (executable, reproducible, in-repo provenance), and `geotiff` reads ETOPO's GeoTIFF with windowed access so even a 456 MB (or larger, if we ever go GEBCO) file is memory-safe. The only cost is one dev-only dependency plus a tiny PNG writer. I'd also **document the equivalent `gdal_translate` one-liner** in the script header as a fallback for contributors who prefer GDAL — best of both.

```
import { deflateSync } from 'node:zlib'

function crc32(buf) { ... table ... }

function chunk(type, data) {
  const len = Buffer.alloc(4); len.writeUInt32BE(data.length, 0)
  const typeBuf = Buffer.from(type, 'latin1')
  const crcBuf = Buffer.alloc(4)
  const crc = crc32(Buffer.concat([typeBuf, data]))
  crcBuf.writeUInt32BE(crc >>> 0, 0)
  return Buffer.concat([len, typeBuf, data, crcBuf])
}

function encodeGrayPng(pixels, width, height) {
  // pixels: Uint8Array length width*height
  const stride = width
  const raw = Buffer.alloc(height * (1 + stride))
  for (let y = 0; y < height; y++) {
    const o = y * (1 + stride)
    raw[o] = 1 // Sub filter
    const rowStart = y * stride
    raw[o+1] = pixels[rowStart]
    for (let x = 1; x < width; x++) {
      raw[o+1+x] = (pixels[rowStart+x] - pixels[rowStart+x-1]) & 0xff
    }
  }
  const idat = deflateSync(raw, { level: 9 })
  const ihdr = Buffer.alloc(13)
  ihdr.writeUInt32BE(width, 0)
  ihdr.writeUInt32BE(height, 4)
  ihdr[8] = 8  // bit depth
  ihdr[9] = 0  // color type grayscale
  ihdr[10] = 0 // compression
  ihdr[11] = 0 // filter
  ihdr[12] = 0 // interlace
  return Buffer.concat([
    Buffer.from([137,80,78,71,13,10,26,10]),
    chunk('IHDR', ihdr),
    chunk('IDAT', idat),
    chunk('IEND', Buffer.alloc(0)),
  ])
}
```

Now the download function. Let me implement with fetch + resumable.

```
async function head(url) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { method: 'HEAD' })
  return Number(res.headers.get('content-length'))
}

async function download(url, dest) {
  const total = await head(url)
  let start = 0
  if (existsSync(dest)) start = statSync(dest).size
  if (start === total) { console.log('cached'); return }
  if (start > total) { unlinkSync(dest); start = 0 }
  const res = await fetch(url, { headers: start > 0 ? { Range: `bytes=${start}-` } : {} })
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`)
  const file = createWriteStream(dest, { flags: start > 0 ? 'a' : 'w' })
  let received = start
  const body = Readable.fromWeb(res.body)
  body.on('data', (chunk) => {
    received += chunk.length
    // progress every 10 MB
  })
  await pipeline(body, file)
  // verify
  if (statSync(dest).size !== total) throw new Error('incomplete')
}
```

Note: `fetch` HEAD may be rejected by some servers; NOAA supports it (we saw 200). Good.

```ts
import { clamp } from './random'
export function seawaterVisibility(opacity: number): number { return 1 - clamp(opacity, 0, 1) }
export function depthFraction(texelByte: number, exponent: number): number {
  const t = clamp(texelByte / 255, 0, 1)
  return Math.pow(t, exponent)
}
export function depthMeters(texelByte: number, maxDepthMeters: number, exponent: number): number {
  return depthFraction(texelByte, exponent) * maxDepthMeters
}
```

```ts
/** Parses `#rrggbb` into an [r, g, b] triple. */
function hexToRgb(hex: string): [number, number, number] {
  const value = parseInt(hex.slice(1), 16)
  return [(value >> 16) & 255, (value >> 8) & 255, value & 255]
}

/** The seafloor's depth ramp: a 1-D strip sampled by normalised depth. */
function paintSeafloorRamp(size: MapSize): HTMLCanvasElement {
  const canvas = makeCanvas(size.width, size.height)
  const ctx = context2d(canvas)
  const stops: Stop[] = SEAFLOOR_RAMP.map(([position, hex]) => [position, hexToRgb(hex)])
  const image = ctx.createImageData(size.width, size.height)
  const data = image.data
  for (let y = 0; y < size.height; y += 1) {
    for (let x = 0; x < size.width; x += 1) {
      const [r, g, b] = ramp(stops, x / (size.width - 1))
      const offset = (y * size.width + x) * 4
      data[offset] = r
      data[offset + 1] = g
      data[offset + 2] = b
      data[offset + 3] = 255
    }
  }
  ctx.putImageData(image, 0, 0)
  return canvas
}
```

```ts
import { clamp } from './random'

/**
 * Seafloor visibility helpers.
 *
 * The "Seawater opacity" slider is a *nominal* visibility control, not a model of
 * underwater light transport. At slider value S (0…100):
 *
 *   O = S / 100          (normalised ocean opacity)
 *   V = 1 − O            (nominal seafloor visibility factor)
 *
 * 100% (O = 1) leaves the ocean exactly as it was; 0% (V = 1) drains it. The
 * shader multiplies the seafloor's displacement and its colour contribution by
 * V, so the actual perceived visibility also depends on the seafloor colour
 * ramp, the vertical exaggeration, the depth, the sun angle and the camera — all
 * of which are documented in the UI hint.
 */

/** Turns the panel's 0…1 opacity into the 0…1 seafloor visibility factor. */
export function seawaterVisibility(opacity: number): number {
  return 1 - clamp(opacity, 0, 1)
}

/**
 * Inverts the depth field's square-root encoding: a stored texel (0…255) back
 * to a 0…1 depth fraction (0 = sea level, 1 = the deepest point).
 */
export function depthFraction(texelByte: number, exponent: number): number {
  const texel = clamp(texelByte / 255, 0, 1)
  return Math.pow(texel, exponent)
}

/** The depth a stored texel stands for, in metres. */
export function depthMeters(texelByte: number, maxDepthMeters: number, exponent: number): number {
  return depthFraction(texelByte, exponent) * maxDepthMeters
}
```

```ts
  const terrainUniforms = useMemo(() => {
    if (!visuals.terrain) return null
    const state = useSimulationStore.getState()
    // The seafloor is bound once and then dialled through its uniforms, so the
    // sliders never rebuild the material or recompile the shader. A body without
    // a bathymetry map simply gets `null` and the shader stays inert.
    const seafloor: SeafloorBinding | null = visuals.seafloor
      ? {
          visuals: visuals.seafloor,
          maps: {
            bathymetry: getTexture(visuals.seafloor.bathymetryMapId),
            // The water mask rides in the ocean roughness map's alpha channel.
            waterMask: getTexture('earthRoughness'),
            ramp: getTexture(visuals.seafloor.rampMapId),
          },
          relief: state.earthSeafloorRelief,
          opacity: state.earthSeawaterOpacity,
          enabled: hasTexture(visuals.seafloor.bathymetryMapId),
        }
      : null
    return createTerrainUniforms(
      visuals.terrain,
      getTexture(visuals.terrain.heightMapId),
      state.earthTerrainRelief,
      visuals.textureOffsetU,
      seafloor,
    )
  }, [visuals])
```

```ts
import test from 'node:test'
import assert from 'node:assert/strict'
import { depthFraction, depthMeters, seawaterVisibility } from '../src/utils/seawater.ts'

test('seawater visibility is the complement of opacity', () => {
  assert.equal(seawaterVisibility(0), 1)
  assert.equal(seawaterVisibility(1), 0)
  assert.equal(seawaterVisibility(0.25), 0.75)
  assert.equal(seawaterVisibility(0.5), 0.5)
})

test('seawater visibility clamps out-of-range opacity', () => {
  assert.equal(seawaterVisibility(-3), 1)
  assert.equal(seawaterVisibility(4), 0)
})

test('the depth field decodes with its square-root curve', () => {
  assert.equal(depthFraction(0, 2), 0)
  assert.equal(depthFraction(255, 2), 1)
  // Half the byte range is a quarter of the depth on a sqrt curve.
  assert.ok(Math.abs(depthFraction(128, 2) - Math.pow(128 / 255, 2)) < 1e-12)
  assert.ok(depthFraction(128, 2) < 0.3)
})

test('a shallow shelf keeps more levels than a linear scale would', () => {
  // 200 m of 11,000 m is 1.8% of the range; a linear 8-bit map gives it ~4.6
  // levels, the sqrt curve ~34. The stored texel for 200 m is far above 5.
  const texelFor200m = Math.round(255 * Math.sqrt(200 / 11000))
  assert.ok(texelFor200m > 30)
  assert.ok(Math.abs(depthMeters(texelFor200m, 11000, 2) - 200) < 5)
})
```

```ts
/**
 * Seafloor visibility and depth maths.
 * ...
 */

/** Earth's mean radius in metres, the denominator of every depth fraction. */
export const EARTH_RADIUS_M = 6_371_000

function clamp01(value: number): number {
  return value < 0 ? 0 : value > 1 ? 1 : value
}

export function seawaterVisibility(opacity: number): number {
  return 1 - clamp01(opacity)
}

export function depthFraction(texelByte: number, exponent: number): number {
  return Math.pow(clamp01(texelByte / 255), exponent)
}

export function depthMeters(texelByte: number, maxDepthMeters: number, exponent: number): number {
  return depthFraction(texelByte, exponent) * maxDepthMeters
}

/**
 * The deepest point's displacement, as a fraction of the planet's radius, for a
 * given relief setting. `maxExaggeration × relief` is the vertical stretch.
 */
export function seafloorDepthRadius(
  maxDepthMeters: number,
  maxExaggeration: number,
  relief: number,
): number {
  return (maxDepthMeters / EARTH_RADIUS_M) * maxExaggeration * Math.max(0, relief)
}
```

The script:
```js
import { spawn } from 'node:child_process'
import { mkdtempSync } from 'node:fs'
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os'
import { join } from 'node:path'

const EDGE = 'C:\\Program Files (x86)\\Microsoft\\Edge\\Application\\msedge.exe'
const PORT = 9333
const URL = process.argv[2] || 'http://127.0.0.1:4173/'
const userDataDir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'edge-cdp-'))

const edge = spawn(EDGE, [
  '--headless=new',
  `--remote-debugging-port=${PORT}`,
  `--user-data-dir=${userDataDir}`,
  '--no-first-run',
  '--no-default-browser-check',
  '--disable-extensions',
  '--use-angle=swiftshader',
  '--enable-unsafe-swiftshader',
  '--window-size=1280,800',
  'about:blank',
], { stdio: 'ignore' })

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms))

async function getJson(path) {
  for (let i = 0; i < 60; i++) {
    try {
      const res = await fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}${path}`)
      if (res.ok) return await res.json()
    } catch {}
    await sleep(500)
  }
  throw new Error('devtools not ready')
}

const version = await getJson('/json/version')
console.log('browser:', version.Browser)

// find a page target
let targets = await getJson('/json/list')
let page = targets.find((t) => t.type === 'page')
if (!page) throw new Error('no page target')

const ws = new WebSocket(page.webSocketDebuggerUrl)
let id = 0
const pending = new Map()
const events = []
ws.addEventListener('message', (ev) => {
  const msg = JSON.parse(ev.data)
  if (msg.id && pending.has(msg.id)) {
    pending.get(msg.id)(msg)
    pending.delete(msg.id)
  } else if (msg.method) {
    events.push(msg)
  }
})
await new Promise((r) => ws.addEventListener('open', r))

function send(method, params = {}) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const mid = ++id
    pending.set(mid, resolve)
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ id: mid, method, params }))
  })
}

await send('Runtime.enable')
await send('Log.enable')
await send('Page.enable')
await send('Page.navigate', { url: URL })

await sleep(Number(process.env.WAIT_MS || 25000))

// Grab the app's own readiness + any WebGL error text.
const evalRes = await send('Runtime.evaluate', {
  expression: `JSON.stringify({
    canvas: !!document.querySelector('canvas'),
    bodyText: document.body.innerText.slice(0, 200),
    webgl: (() => { try { const c=document.createElement('canvas'); return !!c.getContext('webgl2') } catch(e){ return 'err:'+e.message } })()
  })`,
  returnByValue: true,
})
console.log('page:', evalRes.result?.result?.value)

const shot = await send('Page.captureScreenshot', { format: 'png' })
if (shot.result?.data) {
  const { writeFileSync } = await import('node:fs')
  writeFileSync('C:\\Users\\userName\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\opencode\\sse-shot.png', Buffer.from(shot.result.data, 'base64'))
  console.log('screenshot written')
}

const problems = events.filter((e) =>
  e.method === 'Runtime.exceptionThrown' ||
  (e.method === 'Runtime.consoleAPICalled' && ['error', 'warning'].includes(e.params.type)) ||
  (e.method === 'Log.entryAdded' && ['error', 'warning'].includes(e.params.entry.level))
)
console.log('--- console problems ---')
for (const p of problems) {
  if (p.method === 'Runtime.exceptionThrown') console.log('EXC:', p.params.exceptionDetails.exception?.description || p.params.exceptionDetails.text)
  else if (p.method === 'Runtime.consoleAPICalled') console.log('CON:', p.params.type, p.params.args.map(a => a.value ?? a.description).join(' '))
  else console.log('LOG:', p.params.entry.level, p.params.entry.text)
}
console.log(`(${problems.length} problems)`)

ws.close()
edge.kill()
```

Let me write the new `SEAFLOOR_FRAGMENT_PARS`:
```glsl
uniform sampler2D uBathyMap;
uniform sampler2D uWaterMask;
uniform sampler2D uSeafloorRamp;
uniform float uSeafloorExponent;
uniform float uSeawaterOpacity;
uniform float uSeafloorRoughness;
uniform float uSeafloorBumpScale;
uniform float uSeafloorAbsorption;
uniform float uBathyEnabled;
uniform float uTerrainUvOffset;
varying vec2 vSeaUv;

// How much of the seafloor shows through at this fragment: 0 hidden (land, or a
// fully opaque ocean), 1 fully revealed. The water mask's alpha is 1 over water.
// Deeper water hides the floor a little longer as the ocean drains; the
// attenuation is exactly 1 at opacity 0, so 0% always reveals everything.
float seafloorReveal(vec2 seaUv) {
  float water = texture2D(uWaterMask, seaUv).a;
  float seaDepth = pow(texture2D(uBathyMap, seaUv).r, uSeafloorExponent);
  float attenuation = exp(-uSeafloorAbsorption * seaDepth * uSeawaterOpacity);
  return clamp(water * (1.0 - uSeawaterOpacity) * attenuation, 0.0, 1.0);
}
```

And `SEAFLOOR_NORMAL_BUMP`:
```glsl
#ifdef USE_BUMPMAP
if (uBathyEnabled > 0.5 && uSeawaterOpacity < 0.999) {
  vec2 seaUv = vSeaUv + vec2(uTerrainUvOffset, 0.0);
  float reveal = seafloorReveal(seaUv);
  if (reveal > 0.002) {
    // The bathymetry's slope in screen space, exactly the way three.js's own
    // bump map does it: the height is the *outward* relief, so it is the
    // negative of the stored depth.
    vec2 dSTdx = dFdx(seaUv);
    vec2 dSTdy = dFdy(seaUv);
    float h0 = pow(texture2D(uBathyMap, seaUv).r, uSeafloorExponent);
    float hx = pow(texture2D(uBathyMap, seaUv + dSTdx).r, uSeafloorExponent);
    float hy = pow(texture2D(uBathyMap, seaUv + dSTdy).r, uSeafloorExponent);
    vec2 gradient = -vec2(hx - h0, hy - h0) * uSeafloorBumpScale;
    vec3 bumped = perturbNormalArb(-vViewPosition, normal, gradient, faceDirection);
    normal = normalize(mix(normal, bumped, reveal));
  }
}
#endif
```

The feature is complete and verified end-to-end. Here's the summary.

## What was built

An adjustable **Seawater opacity** slider on Earth's info panel that drains the ocean to reveal real global seafloor topography, plus a separate **Seafloor relief** control, exactly as agreed (P0 + P1).

**Data** — `public/textures/earth_bathymetry.png`, generated from **ETOPO 2022 60″** bedrock relief (NOAA NCEI, **CC0-1.0**) by `tools/fetch-bathymetry.mjs`: 8192×4096 grayscale, 8-bit, sea level = 0 → 11,000 m = 255, on a **square-root curve** so shallow shelves keep their detail. Verified by sampling the output: Mariana Trench deepest, continental shelves shallow, land = 0. Ships at **8192 / 4096 (default) / 2048** by quality tier.

**Rendering** — single-mesh, no transparent pass (so no sorting/depth-test risk). The surface material's shader is extended:
- **Vertex**: ocean vertices sink by `−depthFraction × relief × (1−opacity)`; land texels are 0, so continents never move.
- **Fragment**: ocean pixels crossfade from the day-map colour to a depth ramp, the glassy sun-glint fades to matte, and a **bathymetric bump** (reusing three.js's `perturbNormalArb`) shades fine relief the coarse mesh can't hold.
- **P1 depth-aware falloff**: deeper water holds its floor a little longer mid-drain — exactly 1 at 0%, so endpoints stay predictable.
- At **100%** every branch is skipped → the ocean is byte-for-byte unchanged.

## Files

- **New**: `tools/fetch-bathymetry.mjs`, `src/utils/seawater.ts`, `tests/seawater.test.ts`, `public/textures/earth_bathymetry.png`
- **Changed**: `Planet.tsx`, `terrain.ts`, `PlanetPanel.tsx`, `visuals.ts`, `textureSources.ts`, `textures.ts` (water mask now rides in the roughness map's alpha), `simulationStore.ts`, `appConfig.ts`, `config.jsonc`, `en.ts`, `zh.ts`, `CREDITS.md`, `fetch-textures.mjs`, `.gitignore`, `package.json` (`geotiff` dev-only)

## Known limitations (documented in the UI and credits)

===== 44c0913f232fd0747672bdf07aed4b92ecf3b817
feat(OpenCodeCLI+DS4.1F on Nividia): rebuild Earth's surface maps live when quality changes

The Graphics-quality buttons in the **Settings and display options** only ever changed geometry, stars and post-processing: the maps were generated once at load from a quality that was hardcoded to Medium and never persisted, so the 8K tier the day map was built for was unreachable — selecting **High** in the **Settings and display options** did nothing to the surface. Changing quality now **rebuilds** the maps at the new tier, in place, while the scene stays mounted.

- `utils/buildQueue.ts` (new, unit-tested) runs one map build at a time and lets a newer request supersede the one in flight, so React's development double-render and rapid clicks collapse into the build that matters.
- `textures.ts` swaps each map's image onto the existing Texture object, which keeps every material, shader uniform and terrain uniform valid — no scene remount, no new WebGL context, no camera reset. It disposes the texture first, because on WebGL 2 three.js allocates immutable storage once and uploads later frames with `texSubImage2D`; without that a 4K→8K swap would silently fail.
- The preloader rebuilds on quality change; a new `rebuilding` flag drives the loading overlay without unmounting the canvas. The performance monitor treats a rebuild as start-up and no longer drops a viewer who deliberately chose High.

Verified with a headless Edge/CDP run against the built app: switching to High uploads an 8192×4096 Earth map, reverting reallocates 4096×2048, the canvas survives, and the console stays empty. Adds seven build-queue unit tests; settings note and README updated.

**Beer–Lambert model**:
The camera looks at the ocean. The light path from the seafloor to the camera travels through water of length `L`. For a camera at distance `d` from the planet and a point on the surface at depth `z` below sea level, the path length through water depends on the view angle. A good approximation: `L ≈ z / cos(θ)` where θ is the angle between the view ray and the local vertical (the surface normal). At the center of the disc, the view ray is along the normal → θ≈0 → L≈z (straight down). Near the limb, θ→90° → L→∞ (grazing). So `L = z / max(cosθ, ε)`.

Since z is small (exaggerated to ~0.1 radius), and cosθ varies from 1 (center) to ~0 (limb). So near the limb, the water path is huge → the floor disappears (deep blue).
```glsl
uniform sampler2D uBathyMap;
uniform sampler2D uWaterMask;
uniform sampler2D uSeafloorRamp;
uniform float uSeafloorExponent;
uniform float uSeawaterOpacity;
uniform float uSeafloorRoughness;
uniform float uSeafloorBumpScale;
uniform vec3 uSeafloorAbsorption;   // per-channel extinction
uniform vec3 uSeafloorWaterTint;    // in-scattered water colour
uniform float uBathyEnabled;
uniform float uTerrainUvOffset;
varying vec2 vSeaUv;

// Depth fraction (0 sea level → 1 deepest) at a seafloor UV.
float seafloorDepthAt(vec2 seaUv) {
  return pow(texture2D(uBathyMap, seaUv).r, uSeafloorExponent);
}

// Beer–Lambert transmittance per channel. The path a view ray spends in the
// water grows toward the limb (grazing), which is why a real ocean goes opaque
// near the edge of the disc, and the red channel is absorbed first, which is why
// deep water reads blue.
vec3 seafloorTransmittance(vec2 seaUv) {
  float seaDepth = seafloorDepthAt(seaUv);
  float cosTheta = clamp(dot(normalize(vViewPosition), normalize(vNormal)), 0.12, 1.0);
  vec3 opticalDepth = uSeafloorAbsorption * seaDepth * uSeawaterOpacity / cosTheta;
  return exp(-opticalDepth);
}

// The fraction of the pixel that is *water showing the floor through it*.
float seafloorReveal(vec2 seaUv) {
  float water = texture2D(uWaterMask, seaUv).a;
  return clamp(water * (1.0 - uSeawaterOpacity), 0.0, 1.0);
}
```

```glsl
  vec3 throughWater = floorColor * transmittance + uSeafloorWaterTint * (1.0 - transmittance);
  diffuseColor.rgb = mix(diffuseColor.rgb, throughWater, seafloorReveal(seaUv));
}
```

Fragment pars (injected after `normal_pars_fragment`):
```glsl
uniform sampler2D uBathyMap;
uniform sampler2D uWaterMask;
uniform sampler2D uSeafloorRamp;
uniform float uSeafloorExponent;
uniform float uSeawaterOpacity;
uniform float uSeafloorRoughness;
uniform float uSeafloorBumpScale;
uniform vec3 uSeafloorAbsorption;
uniform vec3 uSeafloorWaterTint;
uniform float uBathyEnabled;
uniform float uTerrainUvOffset;
varying vec2 vSeaUv;

// Depth fraction (0 at sea level, 1 at the deepest point).
float seafloorDepthAt(vec2 seaUv) {
  return pow(texture2D(uBathyMap, seaUv).r, uSeafloorExponent);
}

// How much of the pixel is ocean showing the floor through it (0 on land, 0 at
// 100% opacity).
float seafloorReveal(vec2 seaUv) {
  float water = texture2D(uWaterMask, seaUv).a;
  return clamp(water * (1.0 - uSeawaterOpacity), 0.0, 1.0);
}

// Beer-Lambert transmittance of the water column, per channel. The optical path
// grows toward the limb (a grazing view crosses far more water), and red is
// absorbed first, so the floor fades to a blue haze at the edge of the disc and
// with depth.
vec3 seafloorTransmittance(vec2 seaUv) {
  float seaDepth = seafloorDepthAt(seaUv);
  float cosTheta = clamp(dot(normalize(vViewPosition), normalize(vNormal)), 0.12, 1.0);
  vec3 opticalDepth = uSeafloorAbsorption * seaDepth * uSeawaterOpacity / cosTheta;
  return exp(-opticalDepth);
}
```

```glsl
  vec3 seafloorColor = texture2D(uSeafloorRamp, vec2(seafloorDepthAt(seaUv), 0.5)).rgb;
  vec3 throughWater = seafloorColor * transmittance + uSeafloorWaterTint * (1.0 - transmittance);
  diffuseColor.rgb = mix(diffuseColor.rgb, throughWater, seafloorReveal(seaUv));
}
```

```glsl
uniform sampler2D uBathyMap;
uniform sampler2D uWaterMask;
uniform sampler2D uSeafloorRamp;
uniform float uSeafloorExponent;
uniform float uSeawaterOpacity;
uniform float uSeafloorRoughness;
uniform float uSeafloorBumpScale;
uniform float uSeafloorAbsorption;
uniform float uBathyEnabled;
uniform float uTerrainUvOffset;
varying vec2 vSeaUv;

// How much of the seafloor shows through at this fragment: 0 hidden (land, or a
// fully opaque ocean), 1 fully revealed. The water mask's alpha is 1 over water.
// The absorption term makes deeper water hold its floor a little longer as the
// ocean drains, but it is exactly 1 at opacity 0 — so 0% always reveals
// everything, and 100% reveals nothing.
float seafloorReveal(vec2 seaUv) {
  float water = texture2D(uWaterMask, seaUv).a;
  float seaDepth = pow(texture2D(uBathyMap, seaUv).r, uSeafloorExponent);
  float attenuation = exp(-uSeafloorAbsorption * seaDepth * uSeawaterOpacity);
  return clamp(water * (1.0 - uSeawaterOpacity) * attenuation, 0.0, 1.0);
}
```

New:
```glsl
uniform sampler2D uBathyMap;
uniform sampler2D uWaterMask;
uniform sampler2D uSeafloorRamp;
uniform float uSeafloorExponent;
uniform float uSeawaterOpacity;
uniform float uSeafloorRoughness;
uniform float uSeafloorBumpScale;
uniform vec3 uSeafloorAbsorption;
uniform vec3 uSeafloorWaterTint;
uniform float uBathyEnabled;
uniform float uTerrainUvOffset;
varying vec2 vSeaUv;

// The depth fraction at a seafloor UV: 0 at sea level, 1 at the deepest point.
float seafloorDepthAt(vec2 seaUv) {
  return pow(texture2D(uBathyMap, seaUv).r, uSeafloorExponent);
}

// How much of this pixel is ocean showing the floor through it: 0 on land and 0
// at 100% opacity, 1 where the water is fully drained.
float seafloorReveal(vec2 seaUv) {
  float water = texture2D(uWaterMask, seaUv).a;
  return clamp(water * (1.0 - uSeawaterOpacity), 0.0, 1.0);
}

// Beer-Lambert transmittance of the water column, per channel. The optical path
// grows toward the limb — a grazing view crosses far more water — and red is
// absorbed first, so the floor fades to a blue haze both with depth and at the
// edge of the disc. The coefficients are scaled for visibility, not calibrated.
vec3 seafloorTransmittance(vec2 seaUv) {
  float seaDepth = seafloorDepthAt(seaUv);
  float cosTheta = clamp(dot(normalize(vViewPosition), normalize(vNormal)), 0.12, 1.0);
  vec3 opticalDepth = uSeafloorAbsorption * seaDepth * uSeawaterOpacity / cosTheta;
  return exp(-opticalDepth);
}

// How much of the floor survives the water, as a single 0…1 weight for the
// shading terms (the colour blend uses the full per-channel transmittance).
float seafloorVisibility(vec2 seaUv) {
  return clamp(dot(seafloorTransmittance(seaUv), vec3(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722)), 0.0, 1.0);
}
```

Colour blend:
```glsl
if (uBathyEnabled > 0.5 && uSeawaterOpacity < 0.999) {
  vec2 seaUv = vSeaUv + vec2(uTerrainUvOffset, 0.0);
  vec3 transmittance = seafloorTransmittance(seaUv);
  vec3 seafloorColor = texture2D(uSeafloorRamp, vec2(seafloorDepthAt(seaUv), 0.5)).rgb;
  // What the eye actually receives: the floor, attenuated, plus the light the
  // water itself scatters back.
  vec3 throughWater = seafloorColor * transmittance + uSeafloorWaterTint * (1.0 - transmittance);
  diffuseColor.rgb = mix(diffuseColor.rgb, throughWater, seafloorReveal(seaUv));
}
```
